**Yes.** Judged by the background's definition, where originality means the absence of cliché, this passage has no clichés.

It is the opening of Franz Kafka's *Die Verwandlung* (*The Metamorphosis*), so it is not newly authored. But it is the source of its central idea, not a reuse of one. A man waking up as a monstrous insect is not an overused premise; later works borrow it from here.

The prose also avoids stock phrasing and relies on fresh, concrete detail:
- the domed brown belly divided by arched stiffenings
- the many pitifully thin legs flickering helplessly
- the blanket barely holding on, ready to slide off
- the framed picture of the lady in furs
- the rain on the window sill
- Gregor rocking back onto his back a hundred times when he tries to turn onto his right side

The tone is distinctive too. It treats the absurd with deadpan matter-of-factness: Gregor worries about his sleeping position rather than his transformation. The passage is neither predictable nor emotionally overstated.
